What makes a cactus so fascinating?

Thriving even in a desert with almost no water, the cactus is a master of survival. Amazing secrets are hidden behind those pointy spines.

This book brings together all kinds of stories about the cactus, including cactus facts, how a cactus lives, and desert plants.

content.alt: Cactus - Nature and science facts about cacti
content.text:
Nature and science facts about cacti

A cactus stores plenty of water in the water-holding cells inside its stem when it rains, then uses it little by little through the dry season. Its spines are modified leaves that reduce water loss, gather dew, and keep animals away. It also keeps its pores closed during the day and opens them only at night to photosynthesize (CAM), cutting down on water loss. A saguaro cactus can live 150–200 years and grow over 15 meters tall.

Great points to observe together

Point out things like the stem (water storage), the spines (modified leaves), the desert environment, and the flowers that appear after rain. Talking about "How does it live in a desert with no water?" together is a great place to start.

Parent guide — extending into observation and hands-on play

Grow a small potted cactus and watch how it survives "even with only occasional watering." Look at the spines without touching them, and gently press the stem to feel how plump it is (that's the stored water).

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. How does a cactus live without water?
A. It stores water inside its stem and uses it little by little, and it photosynthesizes by opening its pores only at night to reduce water loss.

Q. What are a cactus's spines?
A. They are modified leaves. They reduce water loss, gather dew, and keep animals away.

Q. How can we observe them at home?
A. Grow a small potted cactus with occasional watering, feel its plump stem, and observe the spines (without touching).
